Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Apply explicit corrections to the final stated intent. Preserve meaningful filler-like words and unfinished thoughts. Apply clearly spoken punctuation and list cues. Keep the supplied language.", "input": "last saturday i walked through the shared bicycle shed with leah and martin before the volunteer shift began. the rain had come in from the west overnight and there was a narrow wet strip under the back wall, but the floor near the entrance was dry. we moved the two cardboard boxes of old flyers onto the shelf above the recycling bin so nobody would catch a pedal on them. leah had brought a small ruler and checked the gap beneath the side door; it was just under two centimeters at the widest point. martin said the draft was why the paper labels had curled, though the labels on the upper hooks were still flat. i wrote the time as eight forty on the clipboard because the shed clock was six minutes fast.

uh the first thing we looked at was the key board by the entrance. there are twelve numbered hooks, but hook four is empty and hook nine has a blue tag tied to it with string. nora asked if the blue tag was still the spare key and i said right it is the spare, not the pump room tag. that was a real answer because she had put the pump room key on the table beside it. the pump room key has a square green label and opens only the small cupboard beside the sink. joel said he had seen the spare on hook seven on thursday no friday morning, then checked his phone and corrected himself to friday. we marked the move in the log rather than changing the hook numbers.

number one inspect the west wall and record the damp area without moving the timber rack. number two count the helmets on the top shelf and leave the cracked yellow one there until its owner is contacted. number three test the motion light from the doorway and note whether it stays on for at least twenty seconds. number four do not use the red cable tie as a repair for the loose latch because it belongs to the chain stand. leah read that last point aloud from the old task card, and martin said it had been added after the cable tie was cut too short last month. we counted seven helmets, including the yellow one, and the motion light stayed on for twenty three seconds. i left the rack in place because the damp patch was behind it and we could see enough from the aisle.

at the far end of the shed, ren was wiping the pump handle with a cloth. he had written a note in german for his cousin who was collecting a bicycle later, and he explained the two words when i asked. the note said er ist heute nicht da, meaning he is not here today, and um sieben, meaning at seven o clock, referred to the collection time. those words were part of the note, not pauses in what he was telling me. ren said his cousin would come at seven if the bus arrived on time, and he had left the blue bicycle beside the window so it would not block the main aisle. i moved the floor brush away from its front wheel, but did not move the bicycle. the back tyre was flat and the pump gauge showed no reading until ren pressed the valve straight.

we also checked the notice board, where the monthly rota was pinned beneath a clear plastic sleeve. three names had been crossed out in pencil, but the replacement names were written in the margin rather than on the rota itself. leah said, “we should copy those over before sunday, or people will think the evening shift is uncovered.” i asked whether she wanted me to edit the paper copy and she said she would do it after checking with the two volunteers. the small envelope for replacement spoke reflectors was still taped to the lower corner. it held four reflectors and a handwritten price of two euros each; we did not open the envelope. one corner of the plastic sleeve had split, so martin put a note on the supplies list for a new sleeve, size A4, and left the rota where it was.

in the middle aisle we found a silver bell and a pair of damp gloves on the bench. the bell had a strip of masking tape around its clamp, with the words “for the green bike” written in black pen. nobody present knew which green bike the note meant, because there are two, one with a child seat and one with a front basket. we put the bell in the labeled lost property tray and listed the gloves separately because they were not attached to anything. i nearly wrote that both items belonged to the same person, then stopped because there was no name or tag. the gloves were size medium and had a small tear on the left thumb. joel took a photograph of the bench and the two green bicycles so the evening volunteers could compare them with the note.

before we finished, martin checked the side latch three times. it closed if he lifted the door slightly, but it caught on the frame when he let the door swing shut normally. he said, “if the building manager changes the padlock before may first, leave the latch alone until we know whether the new hasp is coming too.” i wrote that condition on the maintenance sheet, and added that the existing padlock still turned with both keys. the manager had not said that a replacement was arranged; the only message on the board asked residents to report a damaged lock. leah measured the hasp plate at four centimeters across and took a picture of the screws. we did not tighten them, because the top screw looked worn and she wanted the manager to see it in place.

as we were leaving, sofia arrived carrying a blue bucket and said “beleza” when i asked whether she had brought the cleaning cloths. she explained that in her family’s casual portuguese it meant something like okay or all good, and then showed me the cloths folded inside the bucket. she had brought three, one gray and two white, and the gray one had a stitched name label reading sofia. the white cloths went into the drawer under the sink, while the gray one stayed with her bucket because she planned to wash it at home. i checked the clipboard again and added the cloth count, the damp patch location, and the note about the latch. the last line said to leave the west wall clear for the next inspection on tuesday afternoon, when leah expects to bring a longer ruler and check whether the wet strip has spread beyond the timber rack.", "output": "Last Saturday I walked through the shared bicycle shed with Leah and Martin before the volunteer shift began. The rain had come in from the west overnight, and there was a narrow wet strip under the back wall, but the floor near the entrance was dry. We moved the two cardboard boxes of old flyers onto the shelf above the recycling bin so nobody would catch a pedal on them. Leah had brought a small ruler and checked the gap beneath the side door; it was just under two centimeters at the widest point. Martin said the draft was why the paper labels had curled, though the labels on the upper hooks were still flat. I wrote the time as eight forty on the clipboard because the shed clock was six minutes fast.

Uh, the first thing we looked at was the key board by the entrance. There are twelve numbered hooks, but hook four is empty, and hook nine has a blue tag tied to it with string. Nora asked if the blue tag was still the spare key, and I said, “Right, it is the spare, not the pump room tag.” That was a real answer because she had put the pump room key on the table beside it. The pump room key has a square green label and opens only the small cupboard beside the sink. Joel said he had seen the spare on hook seven on Thursday—no, Friday morning, then checked his phone and corrected himself to Friday. We marked the move in the log rather than changing the hook numbers.

1. Inspect the west wall and record the damp area without moving the timber rack.
2. Count the helmets on the top shelf and leave the cracked yellow one there until its owner is contacted.
3. Test the motion light from the doorway and note whether it stays on for at least twenty seconds.
4. Do not use the red cable tie as a repair for the loose latch because it belongs to the chain stand.

Leah read that last point aloud from the old task card, and Martin said it had been added after the cable tie was cut too short last month. We counted seven helmets, including the yellow one, and the motion light stayed on for twenty-three seconds. I left the rack in place because the damp patch was behind it, and we could see enough from the aisle.

At the far end of the shed, Ren was wiping the pump handle with a cloth. He had written a note in German for his cousin, who was collecting a bicycle later, and he explained the two words when I asked. The note said “er ist heute nicht da,” meaning “he is not here today,” and “um sieben,” meaning “at seven o’clock,” referred to the collection time. Those words were part of the note, not pauses in what he was telling me. Ren said his cousin would come at seven if the bus arrived on time, and he had left the blue bicycle beside the window so it would not block the main aisle. I moved the floor brush away from its front wheel, but did not move the bicycle. The back tyre was flat, and the pump gauge showed no reading until Ren pressed the valve straight.

We also checked the notice board, where the monthly rota was pinned beneath a clear plastic sleeve. Three names had been crossed out in pencil, but the replacement names were written in the margin rather than on the rota itself. Leah said, “We should copy those over before Sunday, or people will think the evening shift is uncovered.” I asked whether she wanted me to edit the paper copy, and she said she would do it after checking with the two volunteers. The small envelope for replacement spoke reflectors was still taped to the lower corner. It held four reflectors and a handwritten price of two euros each; we did not open the envelope. One corner of the plastic sleeve had split, so Martin put a note on the supplies list for a new sleeve, size A4, and left the rota where it was.

In the middle aisle, we found a silver bell and a pair of damp gloves on the bench. The bell had a strip of masking tape around its clamp, with the words “for the green bike” written in black pen. Nobody present knew which green bike the note meant, because there are two: one with a child seat and one with a front basket. We put the bell in the labeled lost property tray and listed the gloves separately because they were not attached to anything. I nearly wrote that both items belonged to the same person, then stopped because there was no name or tag. The gloves were size medium and had a small tear on the left thumb. Joel took a photograph of the bench and the two green bicycles so the evening volunteers could compare them with the note.

Before we finished, Martin checked the side latch three times. It closed if he lifted the door slightly, but it caught on the frame when he let the door swing shut normally. He said, “If the building manager changes the padlock before May first, leave the latch alone until we know whether the new hasp is coming too.” I wrote that condition on the maintenance sheet and added that the existing padlock still turned with both keys. The manager had not said that a replacement was arranged; the only message on the board asked residents to report a damaged lock. Leah measured the hasp plate at four centimeters across and took a picture of the screws. We did not tighten them because the top screw looked worn, and she wanted the manager to see it in place.

As we were leaving, Sofia arrived carrying a blue bucket and said, “Beleza,” when I asked whether she had brought the cleaning cloths. She explained that in her family’s casual Portuguese it meant something like “okay” or “all good,” and then showed me the cloths folded inside the bucket. She had brought three, one gray and two white, and the gray one had a stitched name label reading “Sofia.” The white cloths went into the drawer under the sink, while the gray one stayed with her bucket because she planned to wash it at home. I checked the clipboard again and added the cloth count, the damp patch location, and the note about the latch. The last line said to leave the west wall clear for the next inspection on Tuesday afternoon, when Leah expects to bring a longer ruler and check whether the wet strip has spread beyond the timber rack."}]
